keckle.c: KECKLE; when the Cables of a Ship gaul in the Hawse, or the Bolt - ropes do so against the Ship ’ s Quarter, the Seamen wind some small Ropes about them; and this serving of these Ropes is called speckling,

kedgingatsea.c: KEDGING, at Sea, is when a Ship is brought ii or down in a narrow River, the Wind being contrary to the Tide, and yet he is to go with the Tide then they use to fet their Fore - fail, or Fore - top - fail and the Missen, and so let the Ship drive with the Tide, that so they may flat her about; and if Ihe happen to cone over too near the Shoar, they have a small Anchor in the Head of their Boat with a Hawser fattened to it from the Ship, which Anchor they then let fall in the Middle of the Stream, and so wind or turn her Head about, lift - ing the Anchor up again when site is come fully a - bout: This Work is called lodging, or to kedge up a River, and the Anchor made use ol is called the

keel.c: KEEL, is the lowest Piece of Timber in a Ship, in the Bottom of her Hull; one End whereof is at the Stern, the other at the Stem: Into this are all the Ground - Timbers and Hooks fattened, and ol - ted fore and aft. When a Ship hath a deep Keel, Ihe is said to have a Ranp Keel; and this serves well to keep her from rowling; but if he is over - floaty and rowls too much, anew Keel isfometimes put on, called a False Keel,
KEEL - ROPE, a Hair - Rope running between the Keelson and the Keel of a Ship, to clear and Litnber - Holes when they are choaked up with Bal - l & ft & c

keelson.c: KEELSON, the next Piece of Timber in a Ship Ship to her Keel, lying right over it next above the Floor - Timber.

keeper.c: KEEPER of the Great Seal, is a Lord by his Office, and ttiled Lord - Keeper of the Great Seal of England He is one of the King ’ s Privy - Council; through whole Hands pass all Charters, Commifli - ons, and Grants of the King under the Great Seal; Without which Seal all such Instruments by Law are of no force: For the King is, in the interpret - tation of Law, a Corporation, and passeth nothing firmly but under the said Seal, which is as the pub - lick Faith of the Kingdom, in the high Esteem and Reputation justly attributed thereto. This Lord - Keeper hath the fame Place, Authori - ty, Preheminence, Jurifdidtion, Execution of Laws, and all other Customs, Commodities, and Advan - tages, as the Lord - Chancellor of England hath for the Time being. He is constituted by the Delivery of the Great Seal to him. and taking his Oath.

KEEPER of the Privy Seal, is a Lord by his Office, through whose Hands pass all Charters signed by the King, before they come to the Great Seal, and some things which do not pass the Great Seal at all. He is of the King ’ s Privy - Council, and one of the Great Officers of the Kingdom.

keeperorchiefwarden.c: KEEPER, or Chief Warden of the For ell, is he who hath the principal Government of all things belonging to the fame.

kenks.c: KENKS, in the Sea Phrase, are Doublings in a Cable or Rope, when ' tis handed in or out, so that K NE it doth not run smooth; or when any Rope makes Turns, and doth not run smooth and lever in the Block, they fay it makes Kenks.

kennets.c: KENNETS, in a Ship, are mail Pieces of Tim - ber nailed to the Inside of the Ship, unto which the Tacks and Sheets are belayed, ( as they call it; j i. e. fattened.

ketch.c: KETCH, a smaller Vessel, but of the fame Form with a Hoy.

kevelsorchevils.c: KEVELS, or Chevils, are small Pieces of Tim - ber nailed to the Inside of a Ship, unto which the Tacky and Sheets Ate belayed or fattened.

keyinmusick.c: KEY, in Musick, is a certain Tone, whereto every Composition, whether it be long or Ihorr, ought to be fitted or design ’ d: And this Key is said to be either Flat or Sharp, not in refpedfc of its own Nature, but with Relation to the Flat or Sharp Third, which is joined with it: See Musick, Pol. II.

kidneys.c: KIDNEY'S. The Kidneys in Man are ab ’ ways Two in Number, One on each Side, being nearly of the Figure of the French or Kidney - Beans; which latter Name, they take, from being like the, Kidneys. The Length of the Human Kidney is between Four and Five Fingers Breadth. They are about Two Fingers Breadth in Thickness, and Three over. The Right - Kidney ns situated under the Livers the Left under the Spleen. In a Foetus their External Substance is divided into several Lobes joyn ’ d together ' which in Adult Persons become more close,; wherefore in such their Surface. is equal and smooth. They have Two Membranes s One Common from the Peritoneum; the Other Proper. Ulu - ally they are cover ’ d, with a good deal of Fat s Their Colour is of a dark Red. There are several, Lymphatic Vcjfels ob - served in the Kidneys, which discharge them - leaves into Pecquet ’ s B, repository: The Veins go into the Vena Cava; The Arteries come from the Aorta. Those Veins and Arteries are called Emul - gents: They come out from the Kidneys in their hollow Sides ( which lie nearest to the Cava and Aorta ) included in one common Capsula, and are divided into several Branches, which surround the Pelvis. These Branches are again fub - divided into an Infinity of other ielfer ones, which go to the external Parts of the Kidneys, where they inosculate, and form a kind of Net; from which their Extremities coming, terminate also in Infinity of Glands, which are all very small. These Glands are in ' Figure roundifti,, and they compose the outer Substance of the Kid - neys, which is half a Finger thick. From each of them there goes a long small lube; and the Colle & ion of these Tubes compose the inneraioft Substance of the Kidneys. As these Tubules approach the Pelvis, they gather together in little Bundles; whose Ex - tremities piercing the Membrane of the Pelvis, form those little Protuberances on the Inside of the Pelvis, or Cavity in the Middle of the Kidney, which are called the Papilla. This Cavity, or Pelvis, is form ’ d by the Di - natation of the Vreters: It fends out several Ramifications, which divide the Urinary Tubes into Bundles; and which make a fort of Capsula to the Blood Vessels. The Use of the Kidneys is to separate the Urine from the Blood; which by the Motion of the Heart and Arteries is thrust into the emulgent Branches, which carry it to the lit - tle Glands; by whose Means the Serosity be - ing separated, is received by the Orifice of of the little Tubes, which go from those Giapds to the Pelvis; from whence it runs by the Ureters into the Bladder. The Blood which was carried into the Glands, its Particles being too gross to enter into the small excretory Tubes, is brought back., from the Kidneys by the Emulgent Veins, to be mingled with the other Venal Blood in the Cava. The Description of the Vreters, Vesica Vrina - ria, Glandule Pennies, &c. you will find in their proper Places. Dr. Kyi l, in his Animal Secretion, pag.,. judges that the Kjdneys are placed so near the Heart as they are, because Salts arc C. cr - pufeies, which are strongly attracted, and have a molt close Union with the Fluid of - Water: For though the Lungs may divide the Parti - cles of Salt ' one from another, yet still they firm - iy adhere to the Aqueous Humour in which: they fvvim; and therefore they may. likewise at fxrft be drawn off; and he thinks that th t Kidneys could not well have been placed at a greater Di - fiance, to have separated such a Quantity of U - rine as they now do; and that not - only on the account of the great quantities of Blood they receive where they are; but likewise, if they had a more distant Situation, other Particles must have united with the Salts and Aqueous Particles ( as, even in their present Station some terrestrial Par - titles do ) and consequently the Urine could not have been distilled such as it is now; or at lead: but in a small Quantity.

kingdomaterm.c: KINGDOM, a Term used by the Chymifts, who, according to rheir Cant in other things, call the Three Orders of Natural Bodies, Animal, Ve - gelable, and Mineral, by the Name of Kingdom, Thus they would fay, Those Bodies which be long to the Animal Kingdom, abound mostic Vola - latine Salt.

king.c: KING ’ S - BENCH, is the Court or Judgment - Seat, where the King of England was sometimes wont to fit in his own Person; and therefore it was moveable with the Court or King ’ s Houihold, and Called Curia Domini Regis, and Aula Regia, as Gwin reports in his Preface to his Reading; and that there - in, and in the Court of Exchequer, which were the only Courts of the King till Henry the Third ’ s Days, were handled all Matters of Justice, as well Civil as Criminal. This Court of the Kjngs - ldench, was wont Ancient Times to be especially exercised in all Cri - minal Matters and Pleas of the Crown, leaving the handling of private Contracts and Civil Actions to the Common - Pleas, and other Courts.
KING ’ Heads, which are made a little bending, to direct the Sweep or Mold of th tFuttockj and Naval Timbers; for here the Lines which make the Compass and Bearing of a Ship, do begin,
KING - PEICE in any Building, is a Piece of Timber branding upright in the Middle between two principal Rafters, and having Strutts or Braces going from it to the Middle of each Pvafrer.
KING - SILVER, is properly that Money due to the King or Queen in the Court of Common - Pleas pro Licentra concordandi, in refpedf of a Li - hence then granted to any Man for palling a Fine.

knave.c: KNAVE - LINE, is a Rope in a Ship, fattened to the Cross - Trees under the Main or Fore - Top, whence it comes down by the Ties to the Ramhead and there ' tis reeved through a Piece of Wood of about two Foot long, and so is brought to the Ship ’ s Side, and there haled up taught to the Rails., Its Use is to keep the Ties and Hallyards froffi turning about one another, as they are apt to do when new and first used; and therefore after they are a little used and stretched, this Knave - Line is ta - ken away, of no further Use.

KNAVE, is an old Saxon Word for a Man - Servant, and Is so used in E.. St at.. c.. and Verftegan thinks it comes from the. Butch Cnapa, which signifies the fame thing. Cnapa in Saxon also, is a Male - Child or Boy; and in this sense a Knave Child hath been frequently used formerly in contra iftineftion to a Girl; and in this sense W'ickjsff uses the Word in his Translation of Exod... and other places of the Bible. kneck.c: KNECK, in the Sea Language, is the twitting of a Rope or Cable as it is veering out.

knees.c: KNEES, are Pieces of Timber in a Ship bowing like a Knee, which are used to bind the Beams and Futtocks together, being bolted strongly into them both. Hence such Timber as is useful for this Purpose, is called,

knee.c: KNEE - TIMBER: Thus the Cut - water of a Ship, is called, The Knee of the Head.

knettels.c: KNETTELS; so the Seamen call two Pieces of Spun - yarn put together untwisted.

knights.c: KNIGHTS, a - board a Ship, are two Pieces of Timber, in each of which go four Shivers, three “ ' for K N O, K N O for the / Halliards, and one for the Top - Ropes. They are usually shaped into the Form of some Head; one of them standeth aft the Main - mast, and therefore is called the Main - Tonight; the o - ther standeth abaft the Foremast on the second Deck; and this is called the Fore - Knight.

KNIGHTS of the Bath, are an Order of Knights made within the Lifts of the Bath, and Girded with a Sword in the Ceremony of their Creation. They are spoken of in Ed.. c.. For their Antiquity and Manner of Creation, fee Dugdale ' s Description of Worcejlerfhire. They take Place of Kjiights Batchellors, and come after Baronets.

KNIGHTS - FEE, is so much Inheritance as is sufficient yearly to maintain a Kjiight with con - lenient Revenue; which in H. III. ’ s Time was Pounds, Cambd. Brit. p. in. But Sir T ho. Smith in his Bjpub. Anglor. lib.. c.. rateth it at Pounds. And in E -. c.. it appears that such as had Pound in Fee, or for Term of Life, might be compelled to be Kjiights; but this is now repealed by Car.. Stow in his Annals faith, “ There were in England at the “ Time of the Conquest ( others'fay ) “ Knights Fees; whereof the Religious Houses, “ before their Suppression, were possess ’ d of “. ” Some fay a Kjiights - Fee contained, others Plow - lands, or Acres.

KNIGHTS of the Garter, are an Order first Created by King Ed, III.: after the Acquisition of many Greatand Glorious Victories. He fought out of his own Kingdpm, and all over Chfiften - dom for a Number of most Excellent and Noble Persons, to each of which he gave a Blue Gar - ter, deck ’ d with Gold, Pearls, and Precious Stones, with a Buckle of Gold, to be worn only on the Left Leg; a Kirtle, Crown, Cloak, Chape - ron, a Collar, and other Stately and Magnificent Apparel. The Number was, of which the King and his Successors were Ordain ’ d Sovereigns, and the others Companions, or Brethren of the most Noble Order of the Garter. This most Honourable Society is now a Col - lege or Corporation; having a Common - Seal be - longing to it; having, besides the Sovereign, which is Guardian of the Order, and who Go - veins it by himself or Deputy; and besides the Companions or Knights of tbs Garter, Sec - lar Canons, that are Priests, or must be within a year after their Admiifton; Vicars, which must also be Priests; and Poor Knights that have no other Subsistence or Means of Living but the Allowance of this Order. The Bishop of Winton, for the Time being is called Prelate of the Garter the Bishop of Sarum, Chancellor of. the Garter; the Dean of PVindfor, Begifier of the Gar - ter. The Principal King at Arms is called Gar - ter; who is to Manage and Marlhal their So - lemnities at all Inftallations and Annual Feafts. The Vfher of the Garter is also Vjher of the Blaclg - Bjd. By Order of King Charles I. all the Com - pinions of the Garter are to wear on the Left Side of heir upper Garment the Cross of England, en - circled with the Garter and Motto, and with Rays of Silver issuing from thence every way like a Star; whence ’ tis usually called the Star and Garter.

knight.c: KNIGHT - SERVICE was a Tenure, whereby several Lands in this Nation were held of the King, which drew after it Homage, Escuage, Wardship, Marriage, Sc. but taken away by iz Car.. cap.. ! KNOTSjthere are two forts of Knots used at Sea: One they call a Bowlin - Knot, because by this Knot ! the Bowlin - Bridles are fattened to the Crengles This is very fast, and will not flip. The other is a Wale - Kjiot, which is a round Knob or Knot, made with three Strands of a Ropej this Knot serves for the Tops ail - Sheets and Stoppers The Divisions aloof the Log - Line are called Knots: These are usually seven Fathom, or forty two Feet asunder, but they should be Feet and then as many Knots as the Log - Line runs out in half a Minute, so many Miles doth the Ship fail in an Hour; supposing her to keep going at any equal Rate, and Allowing for Yaws, Lee - way, See Log.

kalendarmonth.c: KALENDAR Month, is mentioned in Car. z. cap.. and consists of, or Days ( except February, which never hath more than Days, excepting Leap - Tear, and then has ) twelve of which being those mentioned in the Kalendar, make a Tear which hence is vulgarly express ’ d in the Singular Number, and called a Twelve - Month: But when in the Plural Number we fay Twelve Months, then it ( hall be accounted a Month cf Weeks, which is but Days.

kalendar.c: KALENDAR. There is in use still in Stafford - shire, among the Common People, a very peculiar Kind of Perpetual Kjilendar or Almanack, which Dr. Plott, in his Natural History of that County describes very accurately, and proves to be of ' Danish Invention, and no doubt brought in when the Danes had the Government of this Kingdom. It is called there the Clogg, I suppose from its Form and Matter, being uftially made of a Piece of Wood, squared into four Plane Sides, and with a Ring on the upper End of it, to hang it on a preceding Nail iomewhere in the House. There is some Diversity in the E rm of them, some being more Perfect than others. The sol - lowing Figure, which I borrow from Dr. Plott, represents the Common or Family Clogg where each Angle of the Square Sticky with one Half of each of the flat Sides belonging to it, is express d and this is the most clear and intelligible Form it can well appear in, upon a Flat. On each of the Four Sides are Three Months, the Number of the Days being represented by the Notches; That which begins every Month hav - ing a Patulous Stroke turn ’ d up from it: Every Seventh Notch, being alio of a larger Size, stands for Sunday, which seems to ( hew that the Cycle of the Sun or Dominical Letters, are here committed to Memory the Sundays and other Days here be - ing fix ’ d. Over - against many, of the Notches, whether great or final !, there are placed on the Left Hand several Marks or Symbols, denoting the Golden Number, or Cycle oi the Moon which Number, if under, is represented by so many Points but if it be, then a Line is drawn from the Notch, or Day to which it belongs, with a Hbcff return - ed back against the Course of the Line which seems to be design ’ d to represent V the I man Letter for. If the Golden Number be above and under o, then ’ tis mark ’ d out by the former hooked Line for and with theAddidon of as many Points as make up the Numbed design ’ d: As if it be, there are three Points added to the hooked Line, &c. When the Golden Number is, there is a Cross on the Notch to represent X; And if it be above and under, ’ tis express ’ d by Points as before And if above, by the cross Stroke, Points, and a hook Line for V: When ’ tis, the Line issuing from the Notch for the Day, hath two patulous Crosses, or Strokes, as is plain from the following Figure. And these Numbers are not fet so wildly and confusedly against the Days of the Month as at first fight may appear, but in a Method and Or - der whether you confider them as they immedi - ft ately precede and follow one another, or the Di - fiance interceding each Figure, or the Value, or Denomination for every following Number is made by adding to the preceding and every one, by adding n to the following one still calling away the whole Cycle, when the Addition had exceed it. Thus to which stands against January, add, it makes which stands against the Third Day of the Month to which add again, and it makes whence itself comes to be the following Figure, and the next: on the contrary, if to you add, it makes whence deducting, there remains the Number above it, and so on, c. And for the Distances of the Numbers of the fame Denomination, ’ tis to be noted that they Hand asunder either or Days, interchangeably. Thus after, tyhich stands overagainft the ft of January, at Days distance you will find again at the th of the fame Month and from thence, at Days distance, you will have again fet to the ill of March rand at the Last of March, at Days distance, again, Y y y Note, K A L K A L Note, stands against the i ft of January, be - cause was the Golden Number, when the Fathers of the ' Necene Council settled theTime for the Observation of E after. See Plott, in Loc. cie. On the Right Hand, and issuing from the Notches, are several Infer ip tions and Figures, Hieroglyphically representing the Fefttival Days, by some Actions, Offices, or Endowments of the Saints; or else the VPo ) or Sport in faffiion at the Time of the Year. Thus from the Notch of January. being St. Hillary ’ s Day, issues - u Crofts, the Badge of a Biffiop. From the ist of March an Harp for St, David. Against " june. St. Peter s Day, you have his Keys: And against St. Criftpins Day. a Pair of Shoes. Against Jan.. St. Paul ’ s Day, there is an Ax. - And against June. a Sword for St. John Baptiftt. On Aug. th a Gridiron for St. Lawrence. So a Wheel for St. Katherine, a Star for Epiphany, a True - Lover ' s - ICjiot for St. Valentine ’ s Day, ( ftc. And against Chrifttmas - Day is the old Wasjhailling or C arouftmg - Horn, that the Danes used to make Merry withal at that Time. karitjborcarite.c: KARITJB, or Carite, was the Word used for - merly by the Religious for their belt Conventual Brink, or Strong Beer: ' Because in this they drank their Poculum Caritatis, or Grace Cup Which Grace - Cup it fell was sometime called by the name of Kjirite or Carite.

kerf.c: KERF, is the Notch or Slit that is made by the Saw between two pieces of Wood when they are fawing a sunder.

kernellatus.c: KERNELLATUS, anciently signified Ernbat - telled or Crenelled, i. e. Fortified: And KERNELLARE Domum, was to build a House with such Walls and Towers; which to be allow d to do, was a Favour commonly granted by our Kings after the Demoiilhments of the Cadies.

keystone.c: KEYSTONE in, an Arch, is, placed, at the Top or Vertex of Elliptical or such like hat Arches, to bind the weens of the Arch together.

kintal.c: KINTAL, is a Weight in Merchandise, usual - Iy of about an Hundred Pounds, but something snore cr less, according to the different Customs of different Nations.

knightmiles.c: KNIGHT, Miles, from the Saxon Unite, figni - fies with us a Person that beareth Arms, and who lor Vapour and Martial Conduit is by the Some - reign or his Authority Angled from the Ordinary fort of Gentlemen, and raised to a higher Step or Dignity. This among almost all Nations takes his Name from the Horse, because they used to serve in War on Horseback. Thus the Homans cal - led them Equites; the Italian Word is Cavallieri; the French Chevaliers; the Germans Bjyters; the Spaniards GavaUares, &c. It appears by the Stat. i E.. c. i. That formerly a Gentleman having a full Knights - Fee, and holding his Land by Knight - Service, might be urged by Distress to procure bimfelf to be made Kjiight when he came to full Age: But by Car... no Man can be compelled to take that Order on him. The Manner of making Kjiights, Cambden in his Bri - tannin, shortly expresses in these Words: Nojiris very Temporibtts qui Equeftrem Dignitatem fufeipit, flexis gennibm eduBo Gladio levite in humeri fer - cutitur; Princeps his Verbis Gal / ice effatur: Sois Chevalier au nom de Dieu.
